newsitem.title: ITALY: Reform body proposes overhaul for Italian republic.
newsitem.headline: Reform body proposes overhaul for Italian republic.

text.p: Italy's cross-party constitutional reform commission on Monday approved plans which if passed by parliament would change the face of the country's much-maligned political and electoral system.
Here are the five blocs of recommendations:
FORM OF GOVERNMENT

-- A president should be directly elected and will stay in power six years. He/She can be re-elected only once and will have a large say in the country's foreign and defence policy. The president will have limited powers to dissolve parliament.
-- The prime minister will come from the ranks of the largest parliamentary coalition and will be officially appointed by the president.
FORM OF PARLIAMENT
-- The lower house of parliament will be reduced to 400 members from the current 630, will be elected for five years and will be the main legislative assembly.
-- The senate (upper house) will be cut to 200 members from 315. It will act as a "guarantor" for the lower house.

-- Parliament will be elected on a two-round basis instead of the current one round. Some of the seats will be decided by proportional representation, some by the first-past-the post system and others will be rewarded to the winning coalition in a bid to provide a strong majority.
-- Referendums will only be called if proposers can raise 800,000 signatures instead of the present 500,000.
FORM OF THE STATE
-- The present make-up of regions, provinces and local administrations will remain.
-- The regions will be given autonomy over tax and spending plans. Local administrations will also be able to raise their own taxes.
-- The central state, based in Rome, will have power over 31 set areas, including foreign policy, monetary policy and questions of public order.
EUROPE
-- The regions will be allowed a greater say in decision-making regarding the European Union.
JUSTICE
-- The roles of judges and public prosecutors will be more clearly defined.
-- The magistrates' self-regulating body (the CSM) will be divided into two -- one for judges, the other for prosecutors.

The commission failed to agree on new norms for the Bank of Italy or whether to continue the present system of electing senators for life. These topics will be discussed again when the commission resumes its work in September.
The full recommendations are due to go for ratification to parliament early next year with a public referendum on the eventual draft bill not expected before the autumn of 1998.
